text:
Adviser Calls for Smarter, Greener Future for China's World-Leading Shipping Fleet

A national political adviser has stated that China, which possesses the world's largest maritime fleet, should focus on making its sea transport stronger, smarter, and more environmentally friendly. The remarks were reported by China Daily.

The adviser, a professor at Dalian Maritime University, highlighted the fundamental importance of maritime transport, which handles the majority of international cargo movement. She made these comments during a recent political conference session.

Following research conducted along the coast, the professor has recommended that officials encourage the aligned growth of ecological protection and sustainable shipping. Her proposals aim to cultivate new productive forces in this sector and boost innovative capacity.

She noted being impressed by the operational effectiveness of a very large container ship during a port visit in Zhejiang province. The ship's capacity was described as sufficient to meet the seasonal demand of a major urban population.

The professor pointed to substantial progress in domestic ship construction, citing the completion of aircraft carriers, large LNG carriers, and luxury cruise ships as signs of advancement in high-end manufacturing. Furthermore, the integration of sensors and centralized management systems has provided vessels with enhanced capabilities for real-time information exchange with land-based operations, simplifying navigation and improving efficiency and safety for crews.

Concurrently, efforts are intensifying to develop environmentally sustainable ports and vessels. Several ports, including Tianjin and Qingdao, are involved in initiatives aimed at achieving near-zero carbon emissions. These ports are shifting from fossil fuel power to electricity from renewable sources.

New contracts for eco-friendly ships currently represent a dominant share of the worldwide market. Ships capable of using methanol are already operating, and initiatives for vessels powered by ammonia or fully electric systems are in progress. The professor conveyed a positive outlook for the industry's future, anticipating further technological applications on shipping routes and in ports. She suggested that digital integration would improve the security and robustness of maritime networks, and that intelligent ship systems would enhance the navigation experience.

text:
IMO's Net-Zero Fund: Designing a $12 Billion Climate Finance System for Shipping

The Global Maritime Forum reports that the International Maritime Organisation established a revised greenhouse gas emissions reduction strategy in 2023. This strategy set a decarbonisation pathway for shipping and emphasized the dual objectives of driving an energy transition and enabling a just and equitable transition. The concept of a just and equitable transition holds varied meanings for different nations and stakeholders, potentially involving alternative energy development, adaptation support, or impact mitigation, with large-scale climate finance generally seen as a requirement.

Following this strategy, the IMO developed policy measures intended to drive decarbonisation through a global regulatory approach, resulting in the Net-Zero Framework. While initially set for adoption in October 2025, that decision was postponed by one year, with various policy scenarios still under consideration. The framework's global fuel standard is projected to generate substantial annual revenues, estimated between eleven and twelve billion dollars, if adopted in its current form. These funds are intended to reward zero- and near-zero-emission fuels and to enable a just and equitable transition via a global climate fund for international shipping, currently referred to as the Net-Zero Fund.

Work on the rewards for zero- and near-zero-emission fuels is advancing in informal working groups. However, progress on managing the anticipated revenue remains limited, raising concerns about the challenges such a large financial scale could present. Without clear governance and accountability structures, the collection and disbursement of revenues risk facing legitimacy, efficiency, and equity issues, which could undermine support for the revenue-generating measures. Conversely, a well-designed fund could strengthen political buy-in and play a critical role in delivering a just transition.

Climate finance has become a central topic within the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. A collective goal was set to mobilize one hundred billion dollars per year by 2020, a target later extended through 2025. In practice, mobilized finance has remained below this target, reaching approximately eighty billion dollars annually, with the majority provided through public sources like bilateral agreements and multilateral funds. A central challenge is that the energy transition may remain geographically skewed without targeted intervention, as high-income countries are better positioned to attract capital while lower-income economies face market failures that constrain private finance.

The proposed IMO fund will involve several core design components: the scope of impact areas, the governance model, the recipients of funds, and the delivery mechanisms. These components are interdependent, making the fund a complex mechanism to design. Impact areas eligible for revenue disbursement under the Net-Zero Framework include supporting zero- and near-zero-emission fuels and technologies, climate adaptation, capacity building, and addressing disproportionate negative impacts. Prioritizing different areas influences key considerations; supporting alternative fuels impacts environmental effectiveness, while areas like seafarer support are critical for distributional considerations, a prerequisite for a just transition.

Governance is a central component, determining who makes allocation decisions and under what rules. Two broad approaches are under discussion: full oversight by the IMO, where the regulator manages revenues directly, or collaboration with external climate finance institutions that have existing experience. Full IMO oversight would mean the Marine Environment Protection Committee holds decision-making power, potentially through a separate board. Managing annual revenues of several billion dollars would represent a new function for the IMO, raising institutional feasibility concerns due to the time required to establish necessary systems. Collaboration with external funds could offer greater institutional readiness and speed of deployment.

The recipient structure is another key design component. A top-down model transfers revenues directly to national governments. A bottom-up model allocates funds directly to individual projects. A hybrid approach involves public-private project consortia. Environmental effectiveness is generally higher in bottom-up and hybrid models where funds target specific projects. Cost-effectiveness and potential to mobilize private capital are also greater in these models. Distributional considerations may be better addressed by top-down or hybrid approaches that align with national contexts, though they require robust safeguards.

Delivery mechanisms refer to the financial instruments used to disburse funds. These can include grants, debt financing such as concessional loans or guarantees, equity finance, incentive mechanisms, and technical assistance. Each instrument has different implications for environmental effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, distributional outcomes, and institutional feasibility. Grants can de-risk projects but are expended once. Debt instruments can generate leverage through repayment and recycling but are more complex to administer. The choice of mechanism is closely tied to the governance and recipient models selected.

Design choices across these components are interdependent. For illustration, one configuration pathway could involve an IMO-managed fund providing grants directly to company-led mitigation projects. This could offer strong environmental effectiveness and accountability but may disadvantage less developed countries and pose significant institutional challenges for the IMO. Another pathway could channel revenues to an external fund supporting government-led adaptation through debt financing. This might better serve vulnerable states and be more institutionally feasible but carries sovereign debt risks and has limited potential to mobilize private capital.

Overall, a modular and adaptive design combining multiple governance arrangements, recipient models, and instruments is suggested as a strong pathway to deliver a just and equitable transition while maintaining environmental effectiveness and political viability. Designing a reliable system to manage these funds is considered critical to accelerate the availability of zero-emission solutions and secure the necessary political buy-in and market stability for a global transition.

text:
Green fuels can be competitive in the near future

According to the “Renewable Fuel Economics: An OPEX Illustration Based on Current Costs” report, green fuels can be competitive in the near future. While a vessel fueled by green ammonia currently costs nearly three times as much to operate as a VLSFO-fueled vessel, that premium will decrease rapidly if prices evolve as expected – and if an effective global carbon pricing regime is placed on maritime emissions.

Although shape of any future carbon regime remains under discussion, using the most recent drafting of the IMO Net Zero Framework illustrates the potential impact.

With IMO penalties and surpluses considered a green ammonia-fuelled vessel, using fuel priced in line with Envision’s existing production, would have lower net operating costs than a VLSFO-fueled vessel in the short-term (2029-2036), and lower than an LNG-fueled vessel over the long-term (2029-2050).

Need for further incentivization for e-LNG and green methanol

For e-LNG and green methanol, which currently cost significantly more to produce than green ammonia, further incentivization is needed. This is particularly evident when comparing the cost competitiveness of fossil LNG; even under a regime that penalizes emissions intensity, LNG remains a cost-effective solution compared to those fuels, despite its far lower emissions reduction potential. Any regulatory scheme that aims to encourage maritime decarbonization will need to establish a structure that incentivizes green fuels without making lower carbon but still fossil-based alternatives more attractive.

The report does not factor in a reward for using zero or near zero (ZNZ) emissions fuels, but it would clearly reduce the net cost of all green fuels. A significant reward would be needed for e-LNG and green methanol to compete with VLSFO, while any reward whatsoever would further incentivize green ammonia.

Technology evolution and auxiliary engines

One key area where technology evolution would support lower costs is in auxiliary engines. Today, although methanol and ammonia-fuelled four-stroke engines are promoted, many of the ships being built for these fuels still deploy auxiliaries that run on MDO.

With green fuels used in auxiliary engines, the emissions and carbon costs related to those vessels will be reduced significantly. Another configuration that is already being considered by operators of green fueled vessels is the use of power take-off (PTO) on the main engine to meet electric power demand.

An appropriately sized shaft generator can cover most if not all the auxiliary loads envisioned in this study, meaning that more green fuel is substituted for MDO, at the higher efficiency of the main engine, further reducing carbon exposure. This would also have a notable CAPEX benefit.

The use of PTO, green-fuelled auxiliary engines and indeed other fuel types will be considered in future modelling by WinGD.

Outlook for green fuels and maritime decarbonization

The aim of this study was to show what can be achieved today and in the near future using green fuels. More can be achieved with a global policy framework that recognizes the need for such decarbonization options.

Combined with expected fuel price evolution and technology advances, those incentives will make green ammonia highly competitive as a marine fuel in the coming years, the report concludes.

text:
The study examines Japan’s Carbon Neutral Port Initiative and Yokohama’s Decarbonization Plan as models for the global maritime industry.

BERKELEY, Calif. — A new study, “An analysis of Japan’s Carbon Neutral Port initiative and Yokohama Port and Harbor Decarbonization Plan,” (Japanese translation) from the University of California, Berkeley examines Japan’s innovative approach to decarbonizing maritime ports. Japan’s Carbon Neutral Port (CNP) certification framework and the City of Yokohama’s port decarbonization initiatives represent serious and forward-looking efforts to address the complex challenge of maritime emissions reduction.

The study comes as momentum builds for decarbonization of the international shipping industry, despite recent delays at the International Maritime Organization (IMO). In a period of regulatory uncertainty and rapid technological change, the report underscores the importance of ensuring that certification systems and infrastructure plans continue to evolve in step with emerging fuel pathways, electrification needs and international policy developments.

The Berkeley analysis, commissioned by Pacific Environment, and authored by David Wooley, director of the Environment Center at University of California’s Berkeley’s Goldman School of Public Policy, examines CNP certification initiative and the Port of Yokohama’s comprehensive decarbonization plan. The CNP certification, established by Japan’s Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism in 2025, sets benchmarks for Japanese maritime terminals to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and improve air quality in port communities.

The City of Yokohama’s Port and Harbor Decarbonization Plan, which won the 2025 IAPH Sustainability Award for Climate and Energy, includes 121 projects ranging from harbor craft electrification to next-generation low- and zero-carbon marine fuels. Notably, Yokohama is pioneering the use of “battery-tanker” ships that would transport power from floating offshore wind turbines to shore using vessels filled with batteries.

“Japan’s CNP Certification is a very thoughtfully constructed program that will encourage and enable Japanese maritime terminals to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from port operations,” said David Wooley, director of the Environment Center at University of California, Berkeley’s Goldman School of Public Policy. “In many ways Japan is ahead of other nations on decarbonization of maritime terminals and related industrial operations. The Port of Yokohama serves as a model for other port decarbonization efforts in Japan and will positively influence port decarbonization efforts internationally.”

Across Asia, ports are also advancing their own decarbonization strategies alongside Japan’s CNP initiative. China has expanded shore power deployment at major ports under Ministry of Transport green port policies, Republic of Korea is scaling up Alternative Maritime Power (AMP) infrastructure under the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries’ maritime decarbonization strategy, and Singapore’s Maritime and Port Authority (MPA) is implementing the Maritime Singapore Decarbonization Blueprint 2050, including electrification of harbor craft and development of supply chains for low- and zero-carbon marine fuels. These regional initiatives highlight the growing role of Asian ports in accelerating maritime decarbonization through electrification, alternative fuels and port infrastructure development.

“While the IMO delays action on global shipping emissions, Japan is demonstrating the kind of leadership the world needs,” said Katsunori Hirano, Japan climate specialist at Pacific Environment.” With the launch of Japan’s national CNP certification and the implementation of the Port of Yokohama’s decarbonization plan, Japan is proving that ambitious climate action in the maritime port sector is both necessary and achievable. This report is intended to contribute constructively to this ongoing process. Drawing on the experience of California ports, the analysis identifies opportunities for refinement and coordination to support national and local authorities, as well as industry stakeholders, in strengthening implementation and maintaining Japan’s credibility and competitiveness in sustainable port development.”

Key recommendations for Japan’s CNP

The analysis offers several recommendations to strengthen Japan’s port decarbonization efforts:

Shore power requirements: The CNP recommends but does not require shore power (to allow ships to plug into grid electricity while docked). Shore power should be a mandatory requirement for higher level port ratings under the CNP. Shore power is increasingly being adopted by major ports worldwide.

Electric power infrastructure planning: The CNP could be strengthened by requiring enhanced planning for electric power infrastructure, needed to support growing demand from shore power, cargo handling equipment electrification and future battery-powered coastal shipping.

Sustainable biomass supply chains: Japan’s port decarbonization policy could be strengthened by development of domestic supply chains for sustainable biomass feedstocks needed to produce low- and zero-carbon liquid marine fuels (e.g., green methanol). Japan produces substantial amounts of agricultural and forestry residues that could be used to reduce emissions from vessels calling at Japanese ports.

Methane emissions: The CNP could expand port greenhouse gas inventories and control measures beyond carbon dioxide to include methane emissions. The paper recommends that the CNP could take a more neutral position on liquefied natural gas (LNG) as a maritime fuel, given its significant lifecycle emissions and supply chain constraints.

More frequent updates: Shortening the revision cycle of the certification system from five years to two or three years would enable the CNP to better reflect rapidly changing technologies and practices in maritime decarbonization.

Recommendations for Port of Yokohama

For the Port of Yokohama’s decarbonization plan, the analysis recommends:

Enhanced electric power planning: Port decarbonization plans should ensuring adequate electric power supply infrastructure is planned in parallel with electrification efforts, potentially requiring investment in microgrids, onsite renewable generation and stationary battery storage.

Hydrogen pipeline details: It would be helpful to provide more detail in future plan iterations on the ambitious hydrogen distribution and storage system connecting the port with nearby chemical, refining, steel and power plant facilities.

Alternative fuel development: Future decarbonization plans could include specific milestones to support intercoastal fleet electrification and supply chains for zero-carbon maritime liquid fuels, including and bio-methanol production from sustainable urban and rural biomass (as a cost-effective bridge to e-methanol).

Expanded boundaries for port emission inventories: Yokohama could create a best practice for maritime port emission inventories by including emissions from ocean-going vessels traveling through the port area and hinterland trucking operations. This will provide a more complete picture of port-related emissions, similar to recent actions by California ports.

LNG incentives: Yokohama could consider phasing out port-call incentives for LNG-propelled ships. Instead incentives could better be used for development of domestic supply chains for low or zero-carbon marine fuels.

Air quality hot spots: Short-range dispersion modeling can be to identify air pollution hot spots in neighborhoods near the port and prioritize emission controls in those areas.

The analysis notes that maritime terminals play a critical role not only for trade but also for decarbonizing other industry sectors including refineries, steel, cement and manufacturing. Yokohama’s comprehensive approach, which involves a network of 42 public-private partnerships, demonstrates the potential for local governments to lead the transition to net-zero port operations while creating economic opportunities and protecting public health.

About Pacific Environment

Pacific Environment confronts our most urgent environmental issues by connecting local and global movements, catalyzing policy change and inspiring action for the benefit of people and our planet. Together, we promote a healthy climate, reduce pollution and conserve biodiversity for an equitable and thriving future.

About Center for Environmental Public Policy (CEPP) at the Goldman School of Public Policy (GSPP)

CEPP takes an integrated approach to solving environmental problems. By synthesizing scientific, economic, technical, social, financial and political understanding, CEPP collaborates to support the creation and implementation of public policies based on exacting analytical standards that carefully define problems and match them with the most impactful solutions. CEPP’s primary focus is on climate change, the key environmental challenge of our time.

text:
The International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) Secretary General, Thomas A. Kazakos (pictured), gave the following address at this week’s Extraordinary Session of the IMO Council:

“The International Chamber of Shipping expresses its strongest condemnation of the attacks against commercial vessels operating in the Middle East and the Persian Gulf. These actions pose an unacceptable threat to the safety of international shipping, undermine the stability of global trade and, most significantly, place innocent seafarers at grave risk.

“These attacks have resulted in fatalities and caused serious injury to seafarers, and around 20,000 remain trapped in the affected area. The longer this crisis endures, the greater the strain that these crews will be placed under, as stores begin to deplete, and bunkers reduce. Industry is moving to provide all the support it can, but it is imperative that States work together to ensure that vessels can be resupplied, and crews changed over safely and expediently to allow for continued safe operation of these vessels.

“Furthermore, we call upon all relevant authorities to take immediate and decisive measures to guarantee safe and secure passage for all affected ships. The right to freedom of navigation is paramount and should be protected, and any efforts to safeguard shipping and facilitate its movement should be closely coordinated with the shipping industry to ensure practical, effective outcomes. Transparent communication and collaboration between governments, navies, and industry will be essential to restore confidence and minimise risk.

“Finally, we urge all parties involved to work urgently to de-escalate and swiftly resolve this crisis. The safety of seafarers, the integrity of essential global supply chains, and the stability of international commerce depend on immediate action to bring these hostilities to an end.”

title: NORHyWAY: A large-scale Hydrogen Valley connecting the full value chain
description:
NORHyWAY is a Norwegian industrial initiative that aims to demonstrate how a complete hydrogen value chain can be realised at scale, from production and storage to distribution and end use across maritime transport, heavy-duty mobility and industry.
The NORHyWAY project is a large-scale Norwegian hydrogen initiative led by RENERGY (Renewable Energy Cluster) and SINTEF/HYDROGENi, in collaboration with 16 industrial partners across the energy, maritime, transport, logistics, research, and technology development sectors.
With planned investments of approximately NOK 11.4 billion, NORHyWAY will establish a fully integrated regional value chain for the production, storage, distribution and use of hydrogen.
The project will significantly increase the production of green hydrogen while developing integrated value chains for both maritime and land-based transport.
Geographically, NORHyWAY stretches from Slagentangen in the Oslofjord to Hammerfest in the north, linking several of Norway’s most important industrial hydrogen initiatives into one coordinated system.

The project is coordinated by the innovation company Fremtidens Industri AS.

With planned investments of approximately NOK 11.4 billion, NORHyWAY will establish a fully integrated regional value chain for the production, storage, distribution and use of hydrogen. Supported by EU funding through Horizon Europe, Norway becomes a European demonstration area for how hydrogen can relieve pressure on the power system, reduce emissions and strengthen industrial competitiveness.

Operating at industrial scale

NORHyWAY aims to demonstrate how hydrogen can be deployed at an industrial scale as both an energy carrier and a flexibility resource in the power system. The project will significantly increase the production of green hydrogen while developing integrated value chains for both maritime and land-based transport.

The ambition is to build capacity for 37,081 tonnes of hydrogen per year by 2035, corresponding to CO₂ reductions of up to 345,000 tonnes. This is equivalent to the emissions from more than 109,000 tonnes of diesel.

Geographically, NORHyWAY stretches from Slagentangen in the Oslofjord to Hammerfest in the north, linking several of Norway’s most important industrial hydrogen initiatives into one coordinated system.

Infrastructure and industrial deployment

Through NORHyWAY, the industrial partners will develop and deploy key infrastructure and solutions across the value chain:

H₂ Hub Kristiansund and H₂ Hub Slagentangen, providing complete infrastructure for maritime use, industry and heavy transport

Additional production facilities, including Hammerfest, and further development of the plant in Bodø

Scaling of Norway’s first pilot projects for hydrogen-powered vessels in the North Sea region

Transport corridors and refuelling infrastructure for long-distance hydrogen trucks

Solutions for using hydrogen to reduce bottlenecks and increase flexibility in the power grid

Part of Europe’s hydrogen ecosystem

Through Horizon Europe, NORHyWAY is part of the EU’s broader hydrogen ecosystem and is linked to the Clean Hydrogen Partnership, Hydrogen Europe and other European Hydrogen Valleys.

NORHyWAY aims to serve as a reference project for developing a competitive market for zero-emission fuels in Europe.

The project is supported by the Clean Hydrogen Partnership and its members.
